title: What did we actually build?
summary: The users and stack; inherited capability versus GC2 work.
opening_answer: We built FlickPond into a reusable cloud video-processing platform. An owner uploads a video, conversion runs in the background, and the owner follows status and plays the result. Browser and Publisher CLI share one public contract. GC2 separated responsibilities, ran on AWS, proved reuse, and made delivery and recovery repeatable.

sections.title: Start with a person, not an AWS diagram

blocks.text: Maya has a folder of training clips. She wants usable videos, a result per file, and retry of a failed conversion without re-uploading. Arun wants the same for one browser video. Neither should run FFmpeg, queues or storage permissions.
The app accepts an upload and records a job, a background worker converts it, and the client asks for status. Acceptance means durably accepted, not encoded.

spec.title: What the owner experiences

steps.label: Upload
steps.detail: Reserve, upload to S3, finalize. S3 upload alone is not an accepted job.

steps.label: Track
steps.detail: Returns before encoding ends; owner polls.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: New attempt reuses the accepted source.

spec.caption: A journey, not a promise every job succeeds or yields HLS.

blocks.q: What problem does FlickPond solve in one sentence?
blocks.a: It turns an owner's uploaded video into a trackable, playable result through a reusable API, with no storage or encoding workflow of their own.

blocks.q: Why does the upload response not wait for conversion?
blocks.a: Encoding outlasts a request; durable acceptance plus background work lets the client check progress separately.

sections.title: The languages and tools, one job each

rows: HTTP endpoints; validate requests and responses
Browser UI; no production npm build

blocks.text: Language, framework, database and cloud service are different things: Python is the program, FastAPI the API, PostgreSQL the state, Lambda or Fargate the runtime. Versions need no memorizing.

Frontend is browser JavaScript with vendored playback libraries; Node and Vitest only run tests. Publisher is a Python CLI. Infrastructure is CloudFormation rendered from Python, not Terraform or Kubernetes.

blocks.q: Is the frontend a React or Node server application?
blocks.a: No. It ships HTML, CSS and browser JavaScript; Node only runs tests.

blocks.text: Fictional planning personas, not interview findings. Accounts own their uploads; no shared team ownership, student access, LMS or admin dashboard.

blocks.a: Two clients: browser app and Publisher CLI. Jules is an integrator persona, not a third app.

blocks.text: A platform exposes capability through a stable contract. FlickPond's is owner-scoped intake, processing and output access; browser and Publisher use it over HTTP with no database passwords, queue credentials or encoder copy.
The claim is demonstrated reuse by a second client, not a marketplace or external adoption.

blocks.q: What concrete evidence supports the platform claim?
blocks.a: Browser and independently built Publisher run the same workflow on the published API; boundary tests show Publisher imports no internals and holds no database credentials. A bounded reuse demo.
